cards.title: Contrast as the Core Marketing Principle
cards.summary: Make every ad, email and store asset stand out from the noise by doing the opposite of what the market already sees.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative or email subject lines and unsure whether the idea will get noticed in a crowded feed or inbox.
steps: Audit what the top competitors and top content creators in your niche are already doing — thumbnail style, hook formats, email subject patterns, PDP copy tone.
Ask 'how can I do the exact opposite?' for each element and pick the reversal that still serves your offer.
Apply contrast at the asset level: subject lines, hooks, creative format, even the page layout the customer lands on.
Treat the source's 'mad scientist' framing as a mindset: the goal is not to look like everyone else, it's to break the scrolling or inbox-clearing habit.
caveats: Contrast is the source's opinionated framework, not a measured benchmark; a contrarian format that confuses the buyer can hurt conversion.
Requires knowing the category norm first — contrast without a baseline is just noise.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Purple Ocean: Carve a Segment Inside a Proven Market
cards.summary: Enter a market with proven demand, then narrow to a hyperspecific segment you can own 100% instead of fighting for a slice of a red ocean.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product or angle to launch, or repositioning an existing store into a defensible niche.
steps: Confirm the parent market has proven demand (search trends, existing competing offers) rather than betting on creating new desire.
Identify a narrow slice — demographic, life stage, use case or single angle — where few or no offers specialize.
Build the product and PDP positioning around that slice so the buyer feels it was made specifically for them.

The source's examples: beef organ supplements positioned for women's life stages, nootropics positioned for entrepreneurs, pillowcases positioned around overnight acne. The demonstrated mechanism is the targeting and positioning, not the products themselves.
Accept that you are not inventing a new category — you are transferring existing desire from the proven market into your narrower offer.
caveats: The source calls blue ocean (no competition, no proven demand) and red ocean (proven demand, profits competed away) both bad options; purple ocean is the middle, and the source says it must be created, not found.
Segment size must still be big enough to sustain the offer — the source gives no numeric threshold.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Mass Desire Cannot Be Created, Only Transferred
cards.summary: Stop trying to educate the market into wanting your product; channel an existing desire into your offer instead.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ads or a landing page and wondering whether you need to explain why the customer should care.
steps: Identify the desire your market already holds (from search terms, customer calls, forum language) before writing a single line.
Write copy that connects that existing desire to your product rather than teaching a new problem from scratch.
If your only angle is 'we need to educate people', treat that as a signal to find a proven-demand angle instead.
Use the source's formulation — attributed to Eugene Schwartz — as the decision rule: mass desire can only be transferred, not created.
caveats: This is a direct-response principle the source endorses, not an empirical benchmark; some genuinely new categories have been built, though the source treats that as the rare exception.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Disguise Marketing So It Doesn't Read as an Ad
cards.summary: The highest-performing ad formats work because they don't look like promotions — the same principle behind advertorials, native statics and quiz funnels.
cards.use_when: Designing acquisition creative or landing pages and deciding between obvious ad formats and editorial-style formats.
steps: Balance two moves: contrast to get noticed, and disguise so the customer doesn't feel sold to.
Use formats that read like content — advertorial pages, quiz funnels, native-style ads — while still leading to your offer.
Recognize the principle is decades old (the source cites Gary Halbert's direct-mail observation that people sort mail over the recycling bin) — the format changes, the principle doesn't.
When a format becomes publicly hyped, expect performance to decline as the market floods it; rotate formats while keeping the underlying principle.
caveats: Native/advertorial formats must still comply with platform disclosure rules and local advertising law — the source does not address compliance.
This is the presenter's framework; it is not a guarantee that disguised formats outperform every explicit ad.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Stage-of-Sophistication Check Before Entering a Market
cards.summary: Most markets are at stage four sophistication or later, so an average claim won't work — you need a new mechanism or a new angle.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a product angle or ad claim is strong enough to compete in a saturated category.
steps: Assess the market using the source's stages (attributed to Eugene Schwartz): stage 1 just make a claim, stage 2 compete on bigger claims, stage 3 build a mechanism, later stages require a new angle or identification.
If competitors are already making inflated claims (stage 2–3), do not enter with a slightly better claim — build a distinct mechanism or niche.
Use the cigarette industry as the source's illustrative example of a market passing through every stage; treat that as illustration, not a template.
Combine with purple ocean positioning: the new mechanism is what lets a small operator avoid head-on competition with funded incumbents.
caveats: Stage bands are a source-specific heuristic, not a measured calculation; the source gives no metric for assigning a stage.
The source says 'most markets are stage four or greater' as an opinion, not a measured fact.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: No Clean Hands: Founders Build Their Own Creatives
cards.summary: Founders should manually write copy and build ads in the early stage to develop market intuition, even though it doesn't scale.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to outsource all ad creative and copy at store launch, or to build the first batch yourself.
steps: Write the first ads, hooks, PDP copy and emails yourself rather than delegating everything from day one.
Accept the messy iteration cycle — the source's illustration is a founder testing 50 dropshipping products with zero winners before the skill compounds.
Treat the manual work as market research: every creative you build teaches you how your customer actually reacts.
Only layer in specialists once you personally understand which hooks and angles convert.
caveats: The source's 50-failures story is a personal anecdote, not a required path; the point is reps and intuition, not the specific number.
This conflicts with a pure leverage/outsourcing approach — the source presents it as a deliberate early-stage trade-off, not a permanent rule.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Money Loves Speed: Shrink the Test-to-Iteration Loop
cards.summary: Compress the time between getting early data and shipping the next variation — sometimes to the same day.
cards.use_when: Running paid creative tests or PDP/offer experiments and deciding how fast to iterate after early signal.
steps: Apply the scientific method quickly: question → hypothesis → test → data → next hypothesis.
When a new ad shows early positive indicators with meaningful data, iterate on that ad partway through the same day rather than waiting for a full cycle.
Keep a tight feedback loop on creative, PDP and offer tests so decisions happen on recent data.
The source frames speed as a structural advantage for small operators vs. slow corporate competitors.
caveats: The source conditions iteration on 'positive early signals with significant data' — acting on thin data is the failure mode, not the method.
No specific spend, CTR or CPA threshold is given for 'positive signal'; set your own with enough data to trust it.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Assume Nothing Until the Data Speaks
cards.summary: Every belief about what will convert is an assumption until a test produces data — and ugly creative often wins.
cards.use_when: Choosing between ad concepts, PDP variants or offers, especially when the team has a strong aesthetic preference.
steps: List the assumptions behind each creative or page decision (this will convert, this looks better, this angle is stronger).
Test them rather than debating them; treat only measured outcomes as real.
Expect ugly, low-production creative to sometimes outspend polished work — the source calls this 'ugly ads = pretty profits' and attributes it to clarity beating aesthetics.
Optimize for clarity of message over production value when resources are limited.
caveats: The source's own framing is that ugly ads *often* win, not that polish never matters — a poor-quality ad can also just fail.
Low-production formats must still meet platform policy and brand-safety requirements for your category.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Write Copy to One Stage of Awareness at a Time
cards.summary: Every prospect sits at a different awareness stage; mixing stages in one asset means you're talking to no one.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ad hooks or email flows and deciding how much problem-explanation the piece needs.
steps: Classify the audience stage for the asset: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, or most aware.
Write as if speaking to one hyperspecific person at that stage — do not blend an unaware buyer's framing with a solution-aware buyer's framing in the same piece.
Sequence assets across stages: cold ads speak to problem/unaware, retargeting and email flows speak to product/most aware.
Extract the exact language for each stage from customer research so the copy sounds like the buyer's own words.
caveats: Stages are a copywriting framework the source treats as foundational, not a measured segmentation model.
The source claims you can lead someone from problem aware to product aware, but not speak to unaware and product-aware buyers identically.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Research First: 80% Research, Then Write and Chief
cards.summary: Spend most of the copy process on research from real customer conversations, then write and review with the customer's language.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write a PDP, ad script or email sequence and allocating time across research, drafting and editing.
steps: Allocate roughly 80% of time to research, 5% to writing, 15% to 'chiefing' (reviewing the copy through both the customer's lens and a copywriter's lens) — the source's heuristic.
Prioritize transcripts and calls with your own customers over public forums; the source cites a real customer phrase lifted word-for-word into a top-performing ad hook.
Extract Voice of Customer (VOC) language — the exact phrases buyers use about the problem and desired outcome — and reuse it in hooks and PDP copy.
Use AI deep-research tools to consolidate psychographic and emotional research faster, but still ground it in first-party customer language.
caveats: The 80/5/15 split is the source's rule of thumb, not a measured benchmark.
Public forum research is described as inferior to first-party calls, which requires a system to actually reach customers.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Talk to Your Own Customers for Hook Material
cards.summary: Direct customer conversations produce the most valuable research — specific phrases that become profitable hooks.
cards.use_when: Building a research pipeline for ad hooks, PDP copy or email subject lines and deciding whether forums are enough.
steps: Set up a repeatable process to call or interview customers (the source's team ran calls and reviewed transcripts).
Listen for exact, oddly specific phrases describing the problem — these are candidate hooks.
Test lifted phrases as ad hooks or subject lines; the source reports one customer's exact phrase became one of the most profitable ads in the account.
Use the same transcripts to improve product decisions, not just marketing.
caveats: The source's 'most profitable ad' result is one anecdote, not a guaranteed outcome.
Requires access to customers — early stores with zero buyers must source language another way first.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Hook Anatomy: 80% Copy, 15% Visual, 5% Audio
cards.summary: A video hook is three ingredients — treat the copy as the dominant lever, the scroll stopper as secondary and audio as the smallest needle-mover.
cards.use_when: Producing video ad creative or short-form content and deciding where to spend effort.
steps: Write the first one or two sentences first and hardest — the source weights copy at roughly 80% of hook performance.
Add a scroll stopper (the opening visual) worth about 15%; the test is whether it makes someone say 'what did I just watch?'
Treat audio (voiceover, music) as the smallest mover at roughly 5% — a simple voiceover typically suffices.
Source your scroll stopper from clips that make you and others react viscerally, then test them in ads manager.
caveats: The 80/15/5 weighting is the presenter's stated heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
The 'what did I just watch' test is a source opinion about attention-grabbing visuals; shock value that misrepresents the product can hurt trust and may breach ad policy.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Punch-in-the-Gut Hook Writing
cards.summary: Open with a first line so vivid it feels like a punch, and prioritize clarity over cleverness.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, email subject lines or landing-page headlines where the first line decides whether the rest is read.
steps: Use the PIG framework (punch in the gut, attributed to Chris Haddad): make the first sentence visceral and emotional, good or bad.
During review, repeat the source's editing prompt — 'make this punch harder' — on hooks, subject lines and headlines specifically.
Strip cleverness: if the line is trying to impress, rewrite it to be crystal clear.
Target roughly a fifth-grade reading level (up to eighth grade at most) for hooks and core copy.
Spend disproportionate time here — the source says up to 90% of the effort belongs on the first line/seconds.
caveats: The source's 90% attention figure and reading-level targets are stated rules of thumb, not measured results.
Over-punching without clarity or accuracy can mislead buyers and create refund or policy problems.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Swipe the Philosophy, Not the Words
cards.summary: When borrowing from winning ads, extract the underlying principle and rebuild it for your market instead of rewriting the copy one-to-one.
cards.use_when: Researching competitor or classic ads for inspiration before producing your own creative.
steps: Identify high-performing ads and ask what principle makes them work (contrast, disguise, emotional delta, mechanism).
Do not copy-paste and swap a few words — the source says you learn nothing that way and it only works marginally.
Rewrite from the principle for your specific niche, product and customer language.
Keep a swipe file organized by principle rather than by ad format so you can apply it across ads, emails and PDPs.
caveats: Directly copying competitor copy also carries legal and platform risk — the source advocates principle-level swiping, which avoids this.
This is the presenter's opinion on skill-building; some operators do get short-term lift from close swipes.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Legal Litmus Test for Market Saturation
cards.summary: Once a tactic is being publicly hyped on social media, the source assumes early operators have used it for months or years and it is already getting crowded.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build a store strategy around a tactic or format you just saw trending online.
steps: When a format (native statics, adveditorials, a new creative style) becomes widely discussed, assume adoption is already advanced.
Prefer building on the underlying principle — content that doesn't look like an ad — rather than the specific hyped format.
Watch for declining performance in a format as public discussion rises; rotate to a less-crowded execution.
Use trend tools to separate rising demand (worth entering) from rising tactic chatter (already crowded).
caveats: This is a heuristic from the presenter's experience, not a measured rule; some publicly discussed tactics still work.
The source's claim about performance decline after broad discussion is anecdotal across accounts he observed.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Emotional Delta: Meet Buyers Where They Are, Lift, Then Return
cards.summary: Copy works hardest when it meets the buyer's current emotional state, raises it, then brings them back so the gap drives action.
cards.use_when: Structuring the emotional arc of a sales page, VSL or long-form ad.
steps: Identify the dominant emotional state of the audience (the source uses survival-niche fear as an example).
Open by meeting them there in their own language, rather than starting from an elevated aspirational tone.
Lift the copy toward courage, willingness or relief to show what solving the problem feels like.
Return them to their current reality so the contrast between where they are and where they could be creates the pull to act.
The source's illustration is entrepreneurs who lose wealth a second time feeling it more sharply than the first — that recalled peak makes the return-to-baseline gap acute.
caveats: The 'map of consciousness' framing is the source's own blend of David Hawkins' material with copywriting; it is a creative framework, not an empirical model.
Avoid manufacturing fear or distress in ways that misrepresent the product or exploit vulnerable buyers.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Copy Is Not Content — Separate the Two Functions
cards.summary: Content chases views and engagement; copy chases sales — treat them as opposite ends of a spectrum and don't expect one to do the other's job.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to repurpose social content into ads or sales pages, or how to allocate budget between content and direct-response assets.
steps: Classify each asset: content sits on the brand/engagement end, copy sits on the direct-response/sales end.
Do not assume a popular content piece will convert — the source cites Peter Kell testing VSLs built from content and reporting every one failed.
Build dedicated direct-response copy for anything whose job is sales (PDP, VSL, ad, email offer).
Use content for top-of-funnel attention and audience building, but route sales through purpose-built copy.
caveats: The source says copy is king and claims small audiences with strong copy can outearn larger audiences — an opinionated position, not a measured finding.
Content-driven brands with integrated commerce sometimes do convert content directly; the source treats that as the exception.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Compare Against Your Own Data, Not Other Operators
cards.summary: Comparing early results to other people's highlight reels creates demoralization without improving decisions.
cards.use_when: During a stretch of failed product tests or soft launch performance, when deciding whether to quit or keep iterating.
steps: When a batch of tests fails, review your own results for learning rather than comparing to publicly reported wins.
Expect long dry spells: the source's illustration is 50 failed dropshipping product tests before profitability.

The source also reports a near-overnight reversal — roughly nine months of losses followed by recovery and multiples of it within two to three months — as an example that timing can shift quickly, not as a promise.
Keep decisions anchored on your data and runway rather than on others' timelines.
caveats: 'Trust the process' is motivational framing; it is not a reason to ignore unit economics or to keep funding a failing offer indefinitely.
The $9,000 loss and $20,000 balance are personal anecdotes, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Break the Rule Once You Know It (Contrarian Testing)
cards.summary: Learn the standard marketing rules first, then deliberately test against them — treating dogma as an untested assumption.
cards.use_when: When the team rejects a creative or offer idea because it 'violates best practice'.
steps: Before breaking a rule, verify you know the conventional play and why it exists.
Convert the rule into a testable hypothesis and run it as an experiment rather than accepting it.
Actively test variables others dismiss as silly — the source frames this as the mad-scientist posture.
Use counter-intuitive wins as ego checks that improve calibration.
caveats: The source notes most marketing rules were invented by ordinary practitioners decades ago and then repeated — good reason to test, but not proof the rules never worked.
Rules that are platform policies, legal requirements or safety constraints are not optional to break.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx
